service-1.html: A social post has to communicate at the size people actually see it: on a phone, often between other things competing for attention. I work on static posts, stories, and coordinated designs with a clear hierarchy, so the main idea is easy to find and the piece still belongs to the brand. The packages below separate different amounts of production; the brief establishes the content, source materials, and intended formats.
service-2.html: A carousel needs a sequence, not simply several graphics in the same style. I consider what the first slide introduces, how the following slides develop it, and what the final slide leaves the reader with. Copy placement, pacing, and visual consistency work together. The package scope below describes the production involved, with the supplied material and final formats agreed before work begins.
service-3.html: Editing changes how footage communicates. The first seconds, the choice of shots, the rhythm of a cut, and the relationship between sound and image all affect how a short piece is understood. I edit provided footage and assets for their intended platform, keeping the purpose of the piece in view rather than adding effects simply because they are available.
service-4.html: Content planning connects what a brand wants to communicate with what it can realistically make. I work on directions, topics, and calendars that give individual posts a reason to exist and help different formats support one another. A useful plan should make the next production decision clearer, including the material needed and the kind of content appropriate for each topic.
service-5.html: Creative development begins before a finished visual exists. I research references, look for an angle, and work through how an idea could appear in practice. That includes asking whether the proposed direction suits the audience, the product, and the available production methods. The result should give the next stage of work something specific to respond to.
service-6.html: Research is most useful when it begins with a question. I review competitor, content, and advertising examples to identify patterns relevant to a project, organizing observations so they can inform a discussion. I distinguish what the public material shows from what can only be inferred; an attractive campaign is evidence of a creative choice, not evidence of its financial performance.
service-7.html: Website and brand copy should help a reader understand something specific. I consider what information belongs on the page, how it should be organized, and what tone fits the audience and context. The work involves finding an accurate way to express the idea and revising language that sounds polished without actually communicating much.
service-8.html: Long-form writing needs room for a subject to develop. I work on the angle, supporting material, structure, and transitions that make a longer piece worth reading from beginning to end. Editing is part of that process: checking whether a paragraph advances the idea, whether an example is doing useful work, and whether the conclusion follows from the piece itself.
service-9.html: An email needs to make its purpose clear without asking the reader to work through an entire website first. I consider the entry point, the order of information, and the action the message is intended to support. The wording and structure follow the brief, whether the email introduces something, explains an offer, or continues a conversation with an existing audience.
service-10.html: Search-oriented content still has to be useful to the person who arrives on the page. I work on page content and organization with attention to the subject, the reader’s question, and the clarity of the information. The approved scope below sets out the type of content work included; technical requirements outside that scope are discussed separately.
service-11.html: Content in more than one language needs attention to meaning, register, and context. I consider who will read each version and what needs to remain consistent between them, rather than treating a second language as a mechanical substitution. The brief defines the languages, source material, and intended use. This portfolio interface remains in English.
service-12.html: A visual direction gives a project a consistent basis for making decisions. I work with references, presentation, and the relationship between visual elements to clarify how the work should look and feel. The scope is defined around the actual creative need; developing a direction does not automatically mean that a project needs a complete identity system.
service-13.html: A digital logo or wordmark has to be considered in the places where it will be used. I work within the agreed digital scope, paying attention to clarity, proportion, and how the mark relates to the wider presentation. The packages below explain the deliverables and file limitations so the output is understood before production starts.
service-14.html: A style guide is useful when it helps someone make the next design decision. I organize visual references and usage guidance into a document that explains how a defined direction should be applied. The level of detail depends on the agreed scope and the material already available, with the aim of making the guidance practical to use.
service-15.html: A presentation should make an idea easier to follow. I work on the order of information, the hierarchy within each slide, and the relationship between words and visuals. The design supports the argument rather than competing with it. The brief establishes the source content, audience, intended use, and amount of layout work required.
service-16.html: A landing page gives one offer, project, or campaign a focused place to be understood. I consider what a visitor needs to know first, which information supports that understanding, and how the next action should be presented. The agreed scope defines the content, responsive layout, and any included enquiry or handover requirements.
service-17.html: A portfolio needs to organize work as well as display it. I consider how someone moves between an introduction, selected projects, experience, and a way to get in touch. Project context and readable content matter alongside the visuals. The scope is built around the amount of work being presented and the information visitors need to find.
service-18.html: A business website should make it easy to understand what is offered, find the relevant information, and take a practical next step. I work on the relationship between pages, the organization of content, and the presentation of services or products. The final scope depends on the material available and the functionality the site actually needs.
service-19.html: An e-commerce project needs a closer look at the products, platform, and purchasing requirements before it can be quoted. The work is shaped by how the catalogue is organized, what information a customer needs, and the agreed checkout and operational scope. The packages remain on request because those requirements cannot be established from a single deliverable count.
service-20.html: An additional page needs to fit the website it joins. I consider the purpose of the new content, how it relates to the existing navigation, and which layout patterns should remain consistent. Reviewing the current site and the material for the new page helps establish the actual amount of work before production begins.
service-21.html: Website updates are most useful when they respond to a clear need: information has changed, a new piece of work needs to be added, or part of the experience needs attention. I review the existing site and the requested changes before agreeing on scope. The aim is to improve the relevant area while keeping the rest of the website coherent.
service-22.html: Additional revision work applies when an agreed project needs work beyond its included scope. The original brief, the requested change, and the service involved determine what needs to be done. Corrections to agreed specifications are treated separately from paid additions; the approved package terms below retain that distinction.
service-23.html: Some projects need several kinds of support and do not fit a single package. A combination of research, writing, design, and digital production needs to be scoped around how those parts connect. Send the intended deliverables, source material, and timeframe so the quotation can follow the actual work involved rather than an arbitrary bundle.
service-24.html: UGC production is brand content made for the client’s own channels, whether the piece is on-camera or faceless. The product, intended format, and use of the finished content shape the production brief. Usage licensing, advertising rights, revisions, and additional footage remain separately scoped as described in the approved terms below.
